They can hug the country’s extensive coastline, reaching shallow docks that larger cruise ships cannot. Along the way, passengers have opportunities to meet Norway’s people, experience its traditions, and feel the rhythm of the coast.

Seasonal Wonders

With its spring waterfalls, summer Midnight Sun, autumn foliage, and winter northern lights, Norway delivers wonders year-round. There are many ways to experience them, no matter the season, whether through scenic hikes, cultural encounters, wildlife outings, or more than 130 optional excursions available along the coast.

May and June are known for gushing cascades along the coast, with famous waterfalls like the multi-stream Seven Sisters in Geirangerfjord and Vøringsfossen, one of the country’s most spectacular natural attractions, churning in full force. Spring is also home to Norway’s Constitution Day (May 17th). Marking the day on which the country became an independent kingdom, its festivities include children’s parades, traditional folk costumes (known as bunads) and plenty of hot dogs, ice cream, and waffles.

Come fall, the nights grow longer and there’s a chance of spotting the northern lights. Local Cuisine

Traditional Norwegian cuisine is shaped by the country’s long, cold winters, as well as its coastline. In fact, Hurtigruten’s “Norway’s Coastal Kitchen” is a culinary concept that sources up to 80 percent of its ingredients—such as fish, meats, and cheeses—from local farms, bakeries, and coastal fisheries up and down the shore. On Hurtigruten cruises, every plate tells a story, with pamphlets providing information on the traditions, history, and provenance behind individual dishes. In some restaurants, staff further bring those stories to life by sharing the history and origins of the food directly with guests.

Sweet and caramelly, it’s perfect atop crispbread or waffles. Keep an eye out for fårikål, a mutton and cabbage stew that’s Norway's national dish. It's especially warming and welcoming when temperatures start to drop.
Dramatic Landscapes

Norway has no shortage of spectacular scenery, whether it’s deep fjords tucked amid towering mountains or bright white beaches and sharp peaks that rise straight from the sea. Its small ship size gives Hurtigruten access to some of the country’s most iconic landscapes. Places like Geirangerfjord, a UNESCO-listed fjord brimming with blue waters, surrounded by sheer rock walls, and home to iconic waterfalls such as the Seven Sisters and Bridal Veil; and Trolltunga, a dramatic rock ledge that juts out 2,296 feet at Lake Ringedalsvatnet. Fun fact: its name means “Troll’s Tongue” in Norwegian.

blocks.x: Other jaw-dropping spots include the extraordinary Lofoten Islands and massive Preikestolen (Pulpit Rock), a 1,980-foot-tall cliff sporting breathtaking views. Norway also boasts coastal settings like Flåm, a tiny, postcard-perfect village perched on the arm of the massive Sognefjord, and Bergen. The historic “Gateway to the Fjords,” this walkable and vibrant cultural hub is framed by seven majestic mountains—each of them brimming with hiking paths, stone-step pathways, or forested scrambles.

Whether it's immersing yourself in the culture of coastal communities, dining on foods derived straight from the local landscape, or accessing places off-limits to larger ships, Hurtigruten is your entry into 12,000 years of Norwegian heritage.
